headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: DAL, SPCX, TMUS Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket: SpaceX — Shares were higher by 4% after Grain Management announced it reached an agreement with SpaceX to sell its nationwide 800 megahertz spectrum portfolio. The move that is expected bolster Starlink Mobile's capabilities. Telecom providers – SpaceX's spectrum announcement sent telecom companies lower in premarket trading Friday, as they potentially face increased competition. T-Mobile dropped 7%, AT & T fell almost 6%, and Verizon lost more than 5%. Meanwhile, tower stocks like American Tower and Crown Castle were higher by 6% and almost 8%, respectively. Delta Air Lines — The airline operator fell 4% after it reported weaker-than-expected earnings for the third quarter. Delta earned an adjusted $1.72 per share on revenue of $17.59 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG expected a profit of $1.75 per share on revenue of $17.67 billion. The company said higher fuel costs continue to weigh on its outlook, as it cut its full-year earnings outlook. AI stocks — A slew of companies with exposure to the artificial intelligence buildout were higher in premarket trading Friday after many declined on Thursday following reports that OpenAI's annualized revenue was about $20 billion lower than previously shared. CoreWeave jumped 2.5%, while Oracle and Broadcom rose 1.5%. Lumentum — Shares jumped 6% after the company's CEO Michael Hurlston said that Lumentum's optical components are sold out through 2029. He said Lumentum will struggle to meet as much as 70% demand for some products through next year. Managed care providers — Insurers' shares swung sharply after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services rolled out its 2027 Star Ratings on its Medicare Plan Finder for open enrollment this fall. Shares of Humana surged 14% after the insurer's largest Medicare Advantage contract saw its rating improve. Alignment Healthcare cratered 23%. Apple — Shares were down more than 2% after Nikkei Asia reported that the company was cutting component orders for its iPhone 18 Pro following weaker-than-expected demand. Nikkei added that October production orders for that device and the iPhone 18 Pro Max were cut by 15% from original plans. Park Aerospace — The manufacturer of composite materials for the aerospace market shed earlier gains and traded down 2.5%. Park Aerospace earned 21 cents per share on revenue of $20.8 million in the second quarter. That compares to 12 cents a share and $16.4 million in the year-ago period. Freeport-McMoRan — The miner was up 2.5% as gold prices were on pace for their first positive week in three. U.S. gold futures for December delivery were up 1% on Friday. — CNBC's Darla Mercado and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

headlines.article_text: Ferrari’s chairman is bullish on AI. He’s less certain on monetization Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ferrari chairman John Elkann has rejected concerns about an AI bubble, telling CNBC that a market correction will not derail the technology’s long-term progress. He acknowledged risks stemming from a mismatch between soaring AI infrastructure investment and uncertainty over business revenues. The industrialist told CNBC that European tech companies have the capability to compete with U.S. and Chinese rivals. In this article BSP RACE STLA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:41 04:41 Ferrari chair: I'm not an AI bubble believer Squawk Box Europe Ferrari chairman John Elkann has shrugged off concerns about a potential artificial intelligence bubble — but he warns an AI supply and demand mismatch could pose a risk to markets. In an exclusive interview with CNBC Friday, the billionaire industrialist and Meta Platforms board member, who has invested in technology companies through his family's holding company Exor, expressed optimism for the AI buildout in the decade ahead. Elkann, who is also chairman of auto multinational Stellantis , said the energy and compute requirements for AI-enabled technologies remains high. "What is less certain is what are the revenue-generating mechanisms and business models out of that technology," he said. "That's where you need to see where the mismatch can happen." Elkann said there were different types of bubbles, ranging from those driven purely by financial speculation to those fueled by a rapid buildup of investment and infrastructure. But he said investor focus should remain squarely on the technology's direction of travel. "I am not in the camp of the bubble believers," he said. "Again, I don't think ultimately bubbles, or bursts of bubbles, are going to be an impediment to what progress is, and how it is happening." Speaking to CNBC's Carolin Roth on the sidelines of this year's Wave 2026 technology conference in Turin — formerly known as Italian Tech Week — Elkann said European companies can offer "incredible technical capabilities," amid the increasingly fierce tech battle between the U.S. and China. "The opportunity set ultimately determines where investors will want to go," he observed of the prevailing investment landscape in the continent. "The more opportunities you have, the more capital will come to those opportunities." He highlighted Milan-headquartered conglomerate Bending Spoons — owner of Vimeo, Eventbrite and AOL, among others — as a "perfect example of how one company born in Italy can actually have global ambition, and be able to grow and compete in many different markets as they are doing." He added: "The more of these companies we have, the more will end up having investors backing them."
